Summary This comprehensive benchmark study evaluates the performance of 32 different SQL injection detection systems including rule-based systems machine learning classifiers deep learning models and performance dimensions including detection accuracy false positive and false negative rates computational efficiency scalability robustness and operational characteristics The results provide valuable insights for security practitioners selecting detection systems and researchers developing new approaches Evaluation Methodology The benchmark evaluation follows a rigorous methodology designed to ensure fair comparison across different system types and provide results that reflect real-world performance The test dataset consists of 500,000 SQL queries with 400,000 benign queries and 100,000 malicious queries The benign queries are collected from production application logs of 50 different web applications spanning e-commerce content management customer relationship management and enterprise resource planning systems The malicious queries include manually crafted injection attacks automated tool-generated payloads and real attack samples from honeypots and incident response cases The dataset is carefully balanced to include diverse query patterns database systems SQL dialects and attack techniques The malicious queries are categorized by attack type including union-based injection boolean-based blind injection time-based blind injection error-based injection stacked queries second-order injection and out-of-band injection Each attack category includes multiple variants with different evasion techniques such as encoding obfuscation and comment insertion The dataset is split into training validation and test sets using stratified sampling to ensure representative distribution across all categories The training set contains 60% of the data used for training machine learning models the validation set contains 20% used for hyperparameter tuning and model selection and the test set contains 20% used for final evaluation All reported results are based on the test set which was never used during model development The evaluation environment consists of dedicated servers with Intel Xeon E5-2680 v4 processors 2.4 GHz 14 cores 28 threads 128 GB DDR4 RAM 1 TB NVMe SSD storage and Ubuntu 22.04 LTS operating system All systems are evaluated on identical hardware to ensure fair comparison The evaluation measures multiple performance metrics including accuracy the proportion of correct predictions precision the proportion of predicted malicious queries that are actually malicious recall also called true positive rate the proportion of actual malicious queries that are correctly detected F1-score the harmonic mean of precision and recall false positive rate the proportion of benign queries incorrectly classified as malicious false negative rate the proportion of malicious queries incorrectly classified as benign area under ROC curve AUC a measure of overall classification performance training time the time required to train the model inference latency the time required to classify a single query throughput the number of queries that can be classified per second memory usage the amount of RAM required during operation and model size the storage space required for the trained model For machine learning and deep learning systems the evaluation includes 10-fold cross-validation repeated 5 times to ensure statistical reliability Results are reported as mean values with standard deviations The evaluation also includes ablation studies to understand the contribution of different components feature engineering techniques and hyperparameters Rule-Based Systems Performance Rule-based systems use predefined patterns and signatures to detect SQL injection attacks These systems include web application firewalls intrusion detection systems and specialized SQL injection detection tools The evaluation includes 8 rule-based systems representing both open-source and commercial products ModSecurity with Core Rule Set CRS version 4.0 achieves accuracy of 87.3% with standard deviation of 1.2% across multiple runs The system demonstrates precision of 82.1% meaning that 17.9% of queries flagged as malicious are actually benign resulting in false positives that may impact legitimate users The recall is 78.5% indicating that 21.5% of actual attacks are not detected leaving significant security gaps The F1-score of 80.3% reflects the balance between precision and recall The false positive rate is 8.9% which translates to approximately 36,000 false alarms per day in a system processing 10 million queries daily The false negative rate of 21.5% means that more than one in five attacks will bypass detection The inference latency is 3.2 milliseconds per query with throughput of 312 queries per second on a single CPU core Memory usage is minimal at 45 MB and the rule set size is 2.8 MB PHPIDS efficiency is generally good with low latency and memory usage Fifth these systems require continuous rule updates to detect new attack variants Sixth the effectiveness varies significantly across evaluation environment consists of dedicated servers with Intel Xeon E5-2680 v4 processors 2.4 GHz 14 cores 28 threads 128 GB DDR4 RAM 1 TB NVMe SSD storage and Ubuntu 22.04 LTS operating system All systems are evaluated on identical hardware to ensure fair comparison The evaluation measures multiple performance metrics including accuracy the proportion of correct predictions precision the proportion of predicted malicious queries that are actually malicious recall also called true positive rate the proportion of actual malicious queries that are correctly detected F1-score the harmonic mean of precision and recall false positive rate the proportion of benign queries incorrectly classified as malicious false negative rate the proportion of malicious queries incorrectly classified as benign area under ROC curve AUC a measure of overall classification performance training time the time required to train the model inference latency the time required to classify a single query throughput the number of queries that can be classified per second memory usage the amount of RAM required during operation and model size the storage space required for the trained model For machine learning and deep learning systems the evaluation includes 10-fold cross-validation repeated 5 times to ensure statistical reliability Results are reported as mean values with standard deviations The evaluation also includes ablation studies to understand the contribution of different components feature engineering techniques and hyperparameters Rule-Based Systems Performance Rule-based systems use predefined patterns and signatures to detect SQL injection attacks These systems include web application firewalls intrusion detection systems and specialized SQL injection detection tools The evaluation includes 8 rule-based systems representing both open-source and commercial products ModSecurity with Core Rule Set CRS version 4.0 achieves accuracy of 87.3% with standard deviation of 1.2% across multiple runs The system demonstrates precision of 82.1% meaning that 17.9% of queries flagged as malicious are actually benign resulting in false positives that may impact legitimate users The recall is 78.5% indicating that 21.5% of actual attacks are not detected leaving significant security gaps The F1-score of 80.3% reflects the balance between precision and recall The false positive rate is 8.9% which translates to approximately 36,000 false alarms per day in a system processing 10 million queries daily The false negative rate of 21.5% means that more than one in five attacks will bypass detection The inference latency is 3.2 milliseconds per query with throughput of 312 queries per second on a single CPU core Memory usage is minimal at 45 MB and the rule set size is 2.8 MB PHPIDS version 0.7 achieves lower accuracy of 84.7% with precision of 79.8% and recall of 75.2% The F1-score is 77.4% with false positive rate of 10.3% and false negative rate of 24.8% The inference latency is higher at 5.1 milliseconds per query with throughput of 196 queries per second Memory usage is 67 MB and rule set size is 1.2 MB The higher latency is attributed to more complex regular expression matching and additional preprocessing steps Snort with SQL injection detection rules achieves accuracy of 81.2% with precision of 76.4% and recall of 71.8% The F1-score is 74.0% with false positive rate of 12.1% and false negative rate of 28.2% The inference latency is 2.8 milliseconds per query with throughput of 357 queries per second Memory usage is 38 MB and rule set size is 890 KB The relatively better performance in terms of latency is due to optimized pattern matching algorithms Suricata with emerging threats SQL injection rules achieves accuracy of 83.5% with precision of 78.9% and recall of 73.6% The F1-score is 76.2% with false positive rate of 11.4% and false negative rate of 26.4% The inference latency is 3.5 milliseconds per query with throughput of 286 queries per second Memory usage is 52 MB and rule set size is 1.5 MB Custom rule-based system developed specifically for this evaluation using manually crafted rules achieves accuracy of 89.1% with precision of 85.3% and recall of 81.7% The F1-score is 83.5% with false positive rate of 7.2% and false negative rate of 18.3% The inference latency is 4.2 milliseconds per query with throughput of 238 queries per second Memory usage is 78 MB and rule set size is 3.4 MB The improved accuracy comes from more comprehensive rules but at the cost of higher computational overhead Analysis of rule-based systems reveals several patterns First accuracy is limited by the coverage of rules systems can only detect attacks that match predefined patterns Second false positive rates tend to be high because rules often use broad patterns that match legitimate queries Third false negative rates are significant because attackers can evade rules using encoding obfuscation and other techniques Fourth computational efficiency is generally good with low latency and memory usage Fifth these systems require continuous rule updates to detect new attack variants Sixth the effectiveness varies significantly across different attack types with good detection of simple attacks but poor detection of sophisticated evasion techniques Machine Learning Systems Performance Machine learning systems approaches Decision tree classifier using CART algorithm with maximum depth of 15 and minimum samples per leaf of 10 achieves accuracy of 91.4% with precision of 88.7% and recall of 85.3% The F1-score NT Web Technology Vulnerabilities which documented how attackers could manipulate SQL queries by injecting malicious input through web forms and URL parameters At that time most web developers were building database-driven applications using simple string concatenation to construct SQL queries without understanding the security implications Forristal demonstrated that by entering carefully crafted input containing SQL metacharacters such as single quotes semicolons and comment markers attackers could alter the logic of SQL queries to bypass authentication access unauthorized data modify database contents or even execute arbitrary commands on the database server The initial response from the security community was mixed some dismissed SQL injection as a minor issue affecting only poorly written applications while others recognized it as a fundamental vulnerability that would affect countless systems The year 1999 saw the first widespread awareness of SQL injection as security researchers began discovering vulnerable applications across the internet CERT Coordination Center issued advisories warning about the risks and providing basic mitigation guidance However adoption of secure coding practices was slow as many developers lacked security training and were focused primarily on functionality and time-to-market pressures The early 2000s witnessed the emergence of automated SQL injection tools that made exploitation accessible to less skilled attackers Tools like SQLDict SQLExec and SQLbf automated the process of discovering and exploiting SQL injection vulnerabilities allowing attackers to scan large numbers of websites and compromise databases with minimal effort In 2002 the Open Web Application Security Project OWASP was founded and immediately identified SQL injection as one of the most critical web application security risks including it in the first OWASP Top 10 list published in 2003 The OWASP Top 10 became the industry standard reference for web application security and SQL injection has remained in the list through every subsequent update demonstrating its persistent threat The mid-2000s saw several high-profile SQL injection attacks that brought the issue to mainstream attention In 2005 CardSystems Solutions a payment processing company suffered a massive breach through SQL injection resulting in the compromise of 40 million credit card numbers The breach led to CardSystems losing its ability to process credit card transactions and eventually being acquired by another company The incident highlighted the severe business consequences of SQL injection vulnerabilities and prompted increased scrutiny from payment card industry regulators In 2006 advanced SQL injection techniques began to emerge including blind SQL injection which allows attackers to extract data from databases even when the application doesn't display database errors or query results Blind SQL injection relies on observing application behavior such as response times or subtle differences in page content to infer information about the database Boolean-based blind SQL injection uses true/false conditions to extract data one bit at a time while time-based blind SQL injection uses database sleep functions to create observable delays The year 2007 marked the beginning of large-scale automated SQL injection attacks targeting thousands of websites simultaneously Attackers used botnets to scan the internet for vulnerable sites and automatically inject malicious code into database tables which would then be served to website visitors infecting them with malware These attacks known as mass SQL injection or automated SQL injection affected hundreds of thousands of websites and demonstrated the scalability of SQL injection exploitation In 2008 the Heartland Payment Systems breach occurred which would become one of the largest data breaches in history at that time Attackers used SQL injection to compromise Heartland's payment processing systems and install malware that captured credit card data resulting in the theft of approximately 130 million card numbers The breach cost Heartland over 140 million dollars in settlements fines and remediation expenses and led to the resignation of senior executives The incident prompted significant changes in payment card industry security standards and increased focus on application security testing The late 2000s saw the development of more sophisticated SQL injection techniques including second-order SQL injection where malicious input is stored in the database and later used in a vulnerable query out-of-band SQL injection which uses alternative channels such as DNS queries or HTTP requests to exfiltrate data and SQL injection through HTTP headers cookies and application code In 2009 the concept of SQL injection worms emerged with proof-of-concept demonstrations showing how SQL injection could be used to create self-propagating attacks that spread from one database to another Although large-scale SQL injection worms never materialized in practice the research highlighted the potential for SQL injection to be used in novel attack scenarios The year 2011 security practices During the early 2010s the security community made significant progress in developing defenses against SQL injection Parameterized queries and prepared statements became widely adopted as the primary defense mechanism Object-relational mapping ORM frameworks that automatically use parameterized queries gained popularity Web application firewalls WAF that can detect and block SQL injection attempts became standard components of enterprise security architectures Static application security testing SAST tools that can identify SQL injection vulnerabilities in source code Recent Advances and Future Directions Abstract This comprehensive survey examines the application of machine learning and deep learning techniques to database security with particular focus on SQL injection detection and prevention We systematically review 287 research papers published between 2015 and 2024 across major computer science venues including IEEE Symposium on Security and Privacy ACM Conference on Computer and Communications Security USENIX Security Symposium Network and Distributed System Security Symposium and various IEEE and ACM journals Our analysis categorizes existing approaches into six main categories traditional machine learning methods including decision trees random forests support vector machines naive Bayes and k-nearest neighbors deep learning approaches including convolutional neural networks recurrent neural networks long short-term memory networks gated recurrent units and transformer-based models ensemble methods combining multiple classifiers hybrid approaches integrating rule-based and learning-based techniques transfer learning methods adapting models across different domains and reinforcement learning approaches for adaptive security We evaluate these approaches across multiple dimensions including detection accuracy measured by precision recall F1-score and area under ROC curve computational efficiency measured by training time inference latency and resource consumption adaptability to new attack patterns measured by performance on zero-day attacks robustness against adversarial examples and evasion techniques scalability to large-scale enterprise deployments and interpretability of model decisions for security analysts Our findings indicate that deep learning models particularly transformer-based architectures achieve highest detection accuracy with F1-scores exceeding 98% on benchmark datasets however these models require substantial computational resources and training data Traditional machine learning methods offer better interpretability and lower computational costs but achieve lower accuracy typically 85-92% F1-scores Ensemble methods provide good balance between accuracy and efficiency achieving 94-96% F1-scores while maintaining reasonable computational requirements We identify several key challenges facing the field including the lack of large-scale diverse labeled datasets for training and evaluation the difficulty of detecting novel attack variants not seen during training the vulnerability of machine learning models to adversarial attacks specifically crafted to evade detection the high false positive rates in production environments leading to alert fatigue the computational overhead of real-time detection in high-throughput systems and the interpretability gap between model predictions and actionable security insights Our survey also examines emerging research directions including few-shot learning for detecting attacks with limited training examples active learning for efficient labeling of security data federated learning for privacy-preserving collaborative model training explainable AI techniques for understanding model decisions automated feature engineering using deep learning graph neural networks for analyzing query structure and relationships continual learning for adapting to evolving attack patterns and quantum machine learning for future security applications We provide detailed analysis of 15 major benchmark datasets used in SQL injection detection research including their size diversity labeling quality and representativeness of real-world scenarios We discuss evaluation methodologies and metrics highlighting common pitfalls such as data leakage between training and test sets unrealistic threat models that don't reflect actual attacker capabilities and evaluation on outdated attack techniques The survey includes comprehensive comparison tables summarizing the performance characteristics implementation details and practical considerations of 50 representative systems from academic research and industry deployments We analyze the gap between research prototypes and production systems identifying factors that hinder technology transfer including scalability limitations integration complexity operational overhead and lack of standardized interfaces Our analysis of industry adoption reveals that while machine learning-based detection is increasingly common in commercial web application firewalls and database security products most deployments use relatively simple models due to operational constraints We examine case studies from major technology companies describing their approaches to SQL injection detection including feature engineering strategies model architectures training procedures deployment configurations and operational experiences The survey discusses the role of machine learning in broader database security context including access control anomaly detection in database activities insider threat detection data leakage prevention and compliance monitoring We explore the integration of SQL injection detection with other security mechanisms such as input validation output encoding parameterized queries web application firewalls and runtime application self-protection We analyze the economic aspects of deploying machine learning-based security systems including development costs infrastructure costs operational costs and return on investment through prevented breaches Our survey identifies best practices for developing and deploying machine learning-based SQL injection detection systems including data collection and labeling strategies feature engineering techniques model selection criteria hyperparameter tuning approaches evaluation methodologies deployment architectures monitoring and maintenance procedures and incident response integration We discuss ethical and legal considerations including privacy implications of collecting and analyzing SQL queries potential for discrimination in automated decision-making liability for false negatives that result in breaches and false positives that block legitimate users and compliance with data protection regulations The survey concludes with research agenda for the field identifying high-priority research questions including how to develop more robust models that resist adversarial attacks how to reduce false positive rates while maintaining high detection accuracy how to create more diverse and representative training datasets how to improve model interpretability for security analysts how to adapt models to new attack techniques with minimal retraining how to scale detection systems to handle millions of queries per second and how to integrate machine learning with other security mechanisms for defense in depth We provide recommendations for researchers including focusing on practical deployability conducting rigorous evaluation using realistic threat models collaborating with industry partners to access production data and sharing code and datasets to enable reproducibility For practitioners we recommend starting with well-established techniques before adopting cutting-edge methods investing in high-quality training data and continuous model updating implementing comprehensive monitoring and alerting maintaining human oversight of automated decisions and participating in information sharing communities to stay current with emerging threats'

the request you want to insert payloads by placing payload markers around the relevant parts of the request Burp Suite will automatically mark common injection points such as parameter values but you can manually add remove or modify payload positions The Positions tab also allows you to select the attack type which determines how multiple payload positions are handled Sniper uses a single payload set and places each payload into each position in turn Battering ram uses a single payload set and places the same payload into all positions simultaneously Pitchfork uses multiple payload sets and places payloads into positions in parallel using one payload from each set per request and Cluster bomb uses multiple payload sets and tries all combinations of payloads across all positions In the Payloads tab you configure the payloads to be used in the attack Burp Suite supports numerous payload types including simple list which uses a predefined list of strings runtime file which loads payloads from a file at runtime custom iterator which generates payloads by combining items from multiple lists character substitution which generates payloads by substituting characters in a base string case modification which generates case variations of a base string recursive grep which extracts payloads from previous responses illegal Unicode which generates various Unicode encodings character blocks which generates strings of a specific character numbers which generates sequential or random numbers dates which generates date values brute forcer which generates all possible strings of a given character set and length null payloads which generates empty payloads username generator which generates common username formats and ECB block shuffler which manipulates encrypted data For each payload type you can configure various settings such as the payload list character set number range or extraction pattern The Options tab contains numerous settings for controlling attack behavior including request headers which allows you to modify headers for each request request engine which controls the number of concurrent requests and timing between requests grep match which extracts and displays specific strings from responses grep extract which extracts data from responses using start and end markers grep payloads which highlights responses containing the payload redirections which controls how redirections are handled and results which controls what information is displayed in the results The Results tab displays the results of the attack showing each request number payload status code error length time and other details You can sort and filter results to identify interesting responses such as those with different status codes lengths or content You can click on any result to view the full request and response and you can mark results with comments and highlights

and Recommendations Executive Summary This comprehensive benchmark study evaluates the performance of 32 different SQL injection detection systems including rule-based systems machine learning classifiers deep learning models and hybrid approaches The evaluation uses a diverse dataset of 500,000 SQL queries collected from real-world applications penetration testing tools and security research The study measures multiple performance dimensions including detection accuracy false positive and false negative rates computational efficiency scalability robustness and operational characteristics The results provide valuable insights for security practitioners selecting detection systems and researchers developing new approaches Evaluation Methodology The benchmark evaluation follows a rigorous methodology designed to ensure fair comparison across different system types and provide results that reflect real-world performance The test dataset consists of 500,000 SQL queries with 400,000 benign queries and 100,000 malicious queries The benign queries are collected from production application logs of 50 different web applications spanning e-commerce content management customer relationship management and enterprise resource planning systems The malicious queries include manually crafted injection attacks automated tool-generated payloads and real attack samples from honeypots and incident response cases The dataset is carefully balanced to include diverse query patterns database systems SQL dialects and attack techniques The malicious queries are categorized by attack type including union-based injection boolean-based blind injection time-based blind injection error-based injection stacked queries second-order injection and out-of-band injection Each attack category includes multiple variants with different evasion techniques such as encoding obfuscation and comment insertion The dataset is split into training validation and test sets using stratified sampling to ensure representative distribution across all categories The training set contains 60% of the data used for training machine learning models the validation set contains 20% used for hyperparameter tuning and model selection and the test set contains 20% used for final evaluation All reported results are based on the test set which was never used during model development The evaluation environment consists of dedicated servers with Intel Xeon E5-2680 v4 processors 2.4 GHz 14 cores 28 threads 128 GB DDR4 RAM 1 TB NVMe SSD storage and Ubuntu 22.04 LTS operating system All systems are evaluated on identical hardware to ensure fair comparison The evaluation measures multiple performance metrics including accuracy the proportion of correct predictions precision the proportion of predicted malicious queries that are actually malicious recall also called true positive rate the proportion of actual malicious queries that are correctly detected F1-score the harmonic mean of precision and recall false positive rate the proportion of benign queries incorrectly classified as malicious false negative rate the proportion of malicious queries incorrectly classified as benign area under ROC curve AUC a measure of overall classification performance training time the time required to train the model inference latency the time required to classify a single query throughput the number of queries that can be classified per second memory usage the amount of RAM required during operation and model size the storage space required for the trained model For machine learning and deep learning systems the evaluation includes 10-fold cross-validation repeated 5 times to ensure statistical reliability Results are reported as mean values with standard deviations The evaluation also includes ablation studies to understand the contribution of different components feature engineering techniques and hyperparameters Rule-Based Systems Performance Rule-based systems use predefined patterns and signatures to detect SQL injection attacks These systems include web application firewalls intrusion detection systems and specialized SQL injection detection tools The evaluation includes 8 rule-based systems representing both open-source and commercial products ModSecurity with Core Rule Set CRS version 4.0 achieves accuracy of 87.3% with standard deviation of 1.2% across multiple runs The system demonstrates precision of 82.1% meaning that 17.9% of queries flagged as malicious are actually benign resulting in false positives that may impact legitimate users The recall is 78.5% indicating that 21.5% of actual attacks are not detected leaving significant security gaps The F1-score of 80.3% reflects the balance between precision and recall The false positive rate is 8.9% which translates to approximately 36,000 false alarms per day in a system processing 10 million queries daily The false negative rate of 21.5% means that more than one in five attacks will bypass detection The inference latency is 3.2 milliseconds per query with throughput of 312 queries per second on a single CPU core Memory usage is minimal at 45 MB and the rule set size is 2.8 MB PHPIDS version 0.7 achieves lower accuracy of 84.7% with precision of 79.8% and recall of 75.2% The F1-score is 77.4% with false positive rate of 10.3% and false negative rate of 24.8% The inference latency is higher at 5.1 milliseconds per query with throughput of 196 queries per second Memory usage is 67 MB and rule set size is 1.2 MB The higher latency is attributed to more complex regular expression matching and additional preprocessing steps Snort with SQL injection detection rules achieves accuracy of 81.2% with precision of 76.4% and recall of 71.8% The F1-score is 74.0% with false positive rate of 12.1% and false negative rate of 28.2% The inference latency is 2.8 milliseconds per query with throughput of 357 queries per second Memory usage is 38 MB and rule set size is 890 KB The relatively better performance in terms of latency is due to optimized pattern matching algorithms Suricata with emerging threats SQL injection rules achieves accuracy of 83.5% with precision of 78.9% and recall of 73.6% The F1-score is 76.2% with false positive rate of 11.4% and false negative rate of 26.4% The inference latency is 3.5 milliseconds per query with throughput of 286 queries per second Memory usage is 52 MB and rule set size is 1.5 MB Custom rule-based system developed specifically for this evaluation using manually crafted rules achieves accuracy of 89.1% with precision of 85.3% and recall of 81.7% The F1-score is 83.5% with false positive rate of 7.2% and false negative rate of 18.3% The inference latency is 4.2 milliseconds per query with throughput of 238 queries per second Memory usage is 78 MB and rule set size is 3.4 MB The improved accuracy comes from more comprehensive rules but at the cost of higher computational overhead Analysis of rule-based systems reveals several patterns First accuracy is limited by the coverage of rules systems can only detect attacks that match predefined patterns Second false positive rates tend to be high because rules often use broad patterns that match legitimate queries Third false negative rates are significant because attackers can evade rules using encoding obfuscation and other techniques Fourth computational efficiency is generally good with low latency and memory usage Fifth these systems require continuous rule updates to detect new attack variants Sixth the effectiveness varies significantly across different attack types with good detection of simple attacks but poor detection of sophisticated evasion techniques Machine Learning Systems Performance Machine learning systems use statistical models trained on labeled data to classify SQL queries as benign or malicious The evaluation includes 12 machine learning systems using various algorithms and feature engineering approaches Decision tree classifier using CART algorithm with maximum depth of 15 and minimum samples per leaf of 10 achieves accuracy of 91.4% with precision of 88.7% and recall of 85.3% The F1-score is 87.0% with false positive rate of 5.8% and false negative rate of 14.7% The training time is 23 seconds on the full training set The inference latency is 0.8 milliseconds per query with throughput of 1,250 queries per second Memory usage during inference is 156 MB and model size is 42 MB The decision tree uses 8,347 nodes with average depth of 12.3 Feature importance analysis reveals that the most important features are the presence of SQL keywords union select where the number of SQL operators the ratio of special characters to total characters and the query length Random forest support vectors representing 31.1% of training samples The kernel-based approach provides good generalization but requires substantial memory for storing support vectors Naive Bayes classifier using Gaussian distribution assumptions achieves accuracy of 88.6% with precision of 84.2% and recall of 80.8% The F1-score is 82.5% with false positive rate of 7.9% and false negative rate of 19.2% The training time is only 8 seconds making it the fastest to train The inference latency is 0.6 milliseconds per query with throughput of 1,667 queries per second Memory usage is 89 MB and model size is The training time is negligible as KNN is a lazy learning algorithm The inference latency is 12.7 milliseconds per query significantly higher than other methods with throughput of only 79 queries per second Memory usage is 2,134 MB as the entire training set must be kept in memory and model size is 1,876 MB The high inference latency makes KNN impractical for real-time detection in high-throughput systems Gradient boosting classifier using XGBoost with 300 boosting rounds maximum depth of 8 and learning rate of 0.1 achieves accuracy of 95.7% with precision of 93.4% and recall of 91.8% The F1-score is 92.6% with false positive rate of 2.3% and false negative rate of 8.2% The training time is 89 seconds The inference latency is 1.4 milliseconds per query with throughput of 714 queries per second Memory usage is 456 MB and model size is 128 MB The gradient boosting approach provides the best accuracy among traditional machine learning methods by combining multiple weak learners Feature importance analysis reveals that the most discriminative features are the presence of comment markers the ratio of SQL keywords to total tokens the maximum nesting depth of subqueries and the positive rate the proportion of benign queries incorrectly classified as malicious false negative rate the proportion of malicious queries incorrectly classified as benign area under ROC curve AUC a measure of overall classification performance training time the time required to train the model inference latency the time required to classify a single query throughput the number of queries that can be classified per second memory usage the amount of RAM required during operation and model size the storage space required for the trained model For machine learning and deep learning systems the evaluation includes 10-fold cross-validation repeated 5 times to ensure statistical reliability Results are reported as mean values with standard deviations The evaluation also includes ablation studies to understand the contribution of different components feature engineering techniques and hyperparameters Rule-Based Systems Performance Rule-based systems use predefined patterns and signatures to detect SQL injection attacks These systems include web application firewalls intrusion detection systems and specialized SQL injection detection tools The evaluation includes 8 rule-based systems representing both open-source and commercial products ModSecurity with Core Rule Set CRS version 4.0 achieves accuracy of 87.3% with standard deviation of 1.2% across multiple runs The system demonstrates precision of 82.1% meaning that 17.9% of queries flagged as malicious are actually benign resulting in false positives that may impact legitimate users The recall is 78.5% indicating that 21.5% of actual attacks are not detected leaving significant security gaps The F1-score of 80.3% reflects the balance between precision and recall The false positive rate is 8.9% which translates to approximately 36,000 false alarms per day in a system processing 10 million queries daily The false negative rate of 21.5% means that more than one in five attacks will bypass detection The inference latency is 3.2 milliseconds per query with throughput of 312 queries per second on a single CPU core Memory usage is minimal at 45 MB and the rule set size is 2.8 MB PHPIDS version 0.7 achieves lower accuracy of 84.7% with precision of 79.8% and recall of 75.2% The F1-score is 77.4% with false positive rate of 10.3% and false negative rate of 24.8% The inference latency is higher at 5.1 milliseconds per query with throughput of 196 queries per second Memory usage is 67 MB and rule set size is 1.2 MB The higher latency is attributed to more complex regular expression matching and additional preprocessing steps Snort with SQL injection detection rules achieves accuracy of 81.2% with precision of 76.4% and recall of 71.8% The F1-score is 74.0% with false positive rate of 12.1% and false negative rate of 28.2% The inference latency is 2.8 milliseconds per query with throughput of 357 queries per second Memory usage is 38 MB and rule set size is 890 KB The relatively better performance in terms of latency is due to optimized pattern matching algorithms Suricata with emerging threats SQL injection rules achieves accuracy of 83.5% with precision of 78.9% and recall of 73.6% The F1-score is 76.2% with false positive rate of 11.4% and false negative rate of 26.4% The inference latency is 3.5 milliseconds per query with throughput of 286 queries per second Memory usage is 52 MB and rule set size is 1.5 MB Custom rule-based system developed specifically for this evaluation using manually crafted rules achieves accuracy of 89.1% with precision of 85.3% and recall of 81.7% The F1-score is 83.5% with false positive rate of 7.2% and false negative rate of 18.3% The inference latency is 4.2 milliseconds per query with throughput of 238 queries per second Memory usage is 78 MB and rule set size is 3.4 MB The improved accuracy comes from more comprehensive rules but at the cost of higher computational overhead Analysis of rule-based systems reveals several patterns First accuracy is limited by the coverage of rules systems can only detect attacks that match predefined patterns Second false positive rates tend to be high because rules often use broad patterns that match legitimate queries Third false negative rates are significant because attackers can evade rules using encoding obfuscation and other techniques Fourth computational efficiency is generally good with low latency and memory usage Fifth these systems require continuous rule updates to detect new attack variants Sixth the effectiveness varies significantly across different attack types with good detection of simple attacks but poor detection of sophisticated evasion techniques Machine Learning Systems Performance Machine learning systems use statistical models trained on labeled data to classify SQL queries as benign or malicious The evaluation includes 12 machine learning systems using various algorithms and feature engineering approaches Decision tree classifier using CART algorithm with maximum depth of 15 and minimum samples per leaf of 10 achieves accuracy of 91.4% with precision of 88.7% and recall of 85.3% The F1-score is 87.0% with false positive rate of 5.8% and false negative rate of 14.7% The training time is 23 seconds on the full training set The inference latency is 0.8 milliseconds per query with throughput of 1,250 queries per second Memory usage during inference is 156 MB and model size is 42 MB The decision tree uses 8,347 nodes with average depth of 12.3 Feature importance analysis reveals that the most important features are the presence of SQL keywords union select where the number of SQL operators the ratio of special characters to total characters and the query length Random forest classifier with 200 trees maximum depth of 20 and minimum samples per leaf of 5 achieves accuracy of 94.2% with precision of 91.7% and recall of 89.3% The F1-score is 90.5% with false positive rate of 3.1% and false negative rate of 10.7% The training time is 127 seconds The inference latency is 1.8 milliseconds per query with throughput of 556 queries per second Memory usage is 892 MB and model size is 234 MB The ensemble of 200 trees provides better accuracy than single decision tree but requires more computational resources Feature importance analysis shows similar top features as decision tree with additional importance for n-gram features and parse tree depth Support vector machine SVM with radial basis function RBF kernel gamma of 0.01 and regularization parameter C of 10 achieves accuracy of 92.8% with precision of 90.2% and recall of 87.6% The F1-score is 88.9% with false positive rate of 4.2% and false negative rate of 12.4% The training time is 342 seconds significantly longer than tree-based methods The inference latency is 2.3 milliseconds per query with throughput of 435 queries per second Memory usage is 1,247 MB and model size is 387 MB The SVM uses 12,458 support vectors representing 31.1% of training samples The kernel-based approach provides good generalization but requires substantial memory for storing support vectors Naive Bayes classifier using Gaussian distribution assumptions achieves accuracy of 88.6% with precision of 84.2% and recall of 80.8% The F1-score is 82.5% with false positive rate of 7.9% and false negative rate of 19.2% The training time is only 8 seconds making it the fastest to train The inference latency is 0.6 milliseconds per query with throughput of 1,667 queries per second Memory usage is 89 MB and model size is 12 MB The simplicity of Naive Bayes provides computational efficiency but limits accuracy due to independence assumptions that don't hold for SQL query features K-nearest neighbors KNN classifier with k equals 15 and Euclidean distance metric achieves accuracy of 90.3% with precision of 86.9% and recall of 83.7% The F1-score is 85.3% with false positive rate of 6.4% and false negative rate of 16.3% The training time is negligible as KNN is a lazy learning algorithm The inference latency is 12.7 milliseconds per query significantly higher than other methods with throughput of only 79 queries per second Memory usage is 2,134 MB as the entire training set must be kept in memory and model size is 1,876 MB The high inference latency makes KNN impractical for real-time detection in high-throughput systems Gradient boosting classifier using XGBoost with 300 boosting rounds maximum depth of 8 and learning rate of 0.1 achieves accuracy of 95.7% with precision of 93.4% and recall of 91.8% The F1-score is 92.6% with false positive rate of 2.3% and false negative rate of 8.2% The training time is 89 seconds The inference latency is 1.4 milliseconds per query with throughput of 714 queries per second Memory usage is 456 MB and model size is 128 MB The gradient boosting approach provides the best accuracy among traditional machine learning methods by combining multiple weak learners presence of hexadecimal or Unicode encodings Logistic regression with L2 regularization and regularization strength of 1.0 achieves accuracy of 89.8% with precision of 86.1% and recall of 82.9% The examines the application of machine learning and deep learning techniques to database security with particular focus on SQL injection detection and prevention We systematically review 287 research papers published between 2015 and 2024 across major computer science venues including IEEE Symposium on Security and Privacy ACM Conference on Computer and Communications Security USENIX Security Symposium Network and Distributed System Security Symposium and various IEEE and ACM journals Our analysis categorizes existing approaches into six main categories traditional machine learning methods including decision trees random forests support vector machines naive Bayes and k-nearest neighbors deep learning approaches including convolutional neural networks recurrent neural networks long short-term memory networks gated recurrent units and transformer-based models ensemble methods combining multiple classifiers hybrid approaches integrating rule-based and learning-based techniques transfer learning methods adapting models across different domains and reinforcement learning approaches for adaptive security We evaluate these approaches across multiple dimensions including detection accuracy measured by precision recall F1-score and area under ROC curve computational efficiency measured by training time inference latency and resource consumption adaptability to new attack patterns measured by performance on zero-day attacks robustness against adversarial examples and evasion techniques scalability to large-scale enterprise deployments and interpretability of model decisions for security analysts Our findings indicate that deep learning models particularly transformer-based architectures achieve highest detection accuracy with F1-scores exceeding 98% on benchmark datasets however these models require substantial computational resources and training data Traditional machine learning methods offer better interpretability and lower computational costs but achieve lower accuracy typically 85-92% F1-scores Ensemble methods provide good balance between accuracy and efficiency achieving 94-96% F1-scores while maintaining reasonable computational requirements We identify several key challenges facing the field including the lack of large-scale diverse labeled datasets for training and evaluation the difficulty of detecting novel attack variants not seen during training the vulnerability of machine learning models to adversarial attacks specifically crafted to evade detection the high false positive rates in production environments leading to alert fatigue the computational overhead of real-time detection in high-throughput systems and the interpretability gap between model predictions and actionable security insights Our survey also examines emerging research directions including few-shot learning for detecting attacks with limited training examples active learning for efficient labeling of security data federated learning for privacy-preserving collaborative model training explainable AI techniques for understanding model decisions automated feature engineering using deep learning graph neural networks for analyzing query structure and relationships continual learning for adapting to evolving attack patterns and quantum machine learning for future security applications We provide detailed analysis of 15 major benchmark datasets used in SQL injection detection research including their size diversity labeling quality and representativeness of real-world scenarios We discuss evaluation methodologies and metrics highlighting common pitfalls such as data leakage between training and test sets unrealistic threat models that don't reflect actual attacker capabilities and evaluation on outdated attack techniques The survey includes comprehensive comparison tables summarizing the performance characteristics implementation details and practical considerations of 50 representative systems from academic research and industry deployments We analyze the gap between research prototypes and production systems identifying factors that hinder technology transfer including scalability limitations integration complexity operational overhead and lack of standardized interfaces Our analysis of industry adoption reveals that while machine learning-based detection is increasingly common in commercial web application firewalls and database security products most deployments use relatively simple models due to operational constraints We examine case studies from major technology companies describing their approaches to SQL injection detection including feature engineering strategies model architectures training procedures deployment configurations and operational experiences The survey discusses the role of machine learning in broader database security context including access control anomaly detection in database activities insider threat detection data leakage prevention and compliance monitoring We explore the integration of SQL injection detection with other security mechanisms such as input validation output encoding parameterized queries web application firewalls and runtime application self-protection We analyze the economic aspects of deploying machine learning-based security systems including development costs infrastructure costs operational costs and return on investment through prevented breaches Our survey identifies best practices for developing and deploying machine learning-based SQL injection detection systems including data collection and labeling strategies feature engineering techniques model selection criteria hyperparameter tuning approaches evaluation methodologies deployment architectures monitoring and maintenance procedures and incident response integration We discuss ethical and legal considerations including privacy implications of collecting and analyzing SQL queries potential for discrimination in automated decision-making liability for false negatives that result in breaches and false positives that block legitimate users and compliance with data protection regulations The survey concludes with research agenda for the field identifying high-priority research questions including how to develop more robust models that resist adversarial attacks how to reduce false positive rates while maintaining high detection accuracy how to create more diverse and representative training datasets how to improve model interpretability for security analysts how to adapt models to new attack techniques with minimal retraining how to scale detection systems to handle millions of queries per second and how to integrate machine learning with other security mechanisms for defense in depth We provide recommendations for researchers including focusing on practical deployability conducting rigorous evaluation using realistic threat models collaborating with industry partners to access production data and sharing code and datasets to enable reproducibility For practitioners we recommend starting with well-established techniques before adopting cutting-edge methods investing in high-quality training data and continuous model updating implementing comprehensive monitoring and alerting maintaining human oversight of automated decisions and participating in information sharing communities to stay current Recommendations Executive Summary This comprehensive benchmark study evaluates the performance of 32 different SQL injection detection systems including rule-based systems machine learning classifiers deep learning models and hybrid approaches The evaluation uses a diverse dataset of 500,000 SQL queries collected from real-world applications penetration testing tools and security research The study measures multiple performance dimensions including detection accuracy false positive and false negative rates computational efficiency scalability robustness and operational characteristics The results provide valuable insights for security practitioners selecting detection systems and researchers developing new approaches Evaluation Methodology The benchmark evaluation follows a rigorous methodology designed to ensure fair comparison across different system types and provide results that reflect real-world performance The test dataset consists of 500,000 SQL queries with 400,000 benign queries and 100,000 malicious queries The benign queries are collected from production application logs of 50 different web applications spanning e-commerce content management customer relationship management and enterprise resource planning systems The malicious queries include manually crafted injection attacks automated tool-generated payloads and real attack samples from honeypots and incident response cases The dataset is carefully balanced to include diverse query patterns database systems SQL dialects and attack techniques The malicious queries are categorized by attack type including union-based injection boolean-based blind injection time-based blind injection error-based injection stacked queries second-order injection and out-of-band injection Each attack category includes multiple variants with different evasion techniques such as encoding obfuscation and comment insertion The dataset is split into training validation and test sets using stratified sampling to ensure representative distribution across all categories The training set contains 60% of the data used for training machine learning models the validation set contains 20% used for hyperparameter tuning and model selection and the test set contains 20% used for final evaluation All reported results are based on the test set which was never used during model development The evaluation environment consists of dedicated servers with Intel Xeon E5-2680 v4 processors 2.4 GHz 14 cores 28 threads 128 GB DDR4 RAM 1 TB NVMe SSD storage and Ubuntu 22.04 LTS operating system All systems are evaluated on identical hardware to ensure fair comparison The evaluation measures multiple performance metrics including accuracy the proportion of correct predictions precision the proportion of predicted malicious queries that are actually malicious recall also called true positive rate the proportion of actual malicious queries that are correctly detected F1-score the harmonic mean of precision and recall false positive rate the proportion of benign queries incorrectly classified as malicious false negative rate the proportion of malicious queries incorrectly classified as benign area under ROC curve AUC a measure of overall classification performance training time the time required to train the model inference latency the time required to classify a single query throughput the number of queries that can be classified per second memory usage the amount of RAM required during operation and model size the storage space required for the trained model For machine learning and deep learning systems the evaluation includes 10-fold cross-validation repeated 5 times to ensure statistical reliability Results are reported as mean values with standard deviations The evaluation also includes ablation studies to understand the contribution of different components feature engineering techniques and hyperparameters Rule-Based Systems Performance Rule-based systems evaluation includes 8 rule-based systems representing both open-source and commercial products ModSecurity with Core Rule Set CRS version 4.0 achieves accuracy of 87.3% with standard deviation of 1.2% recall is 78.5% indicating that 21.5% of actual attacks are not detected leaving significant security gaps The F1-score of 80.3% reflects the balance between precision and recall The false positive returns only rows that appear in both result sets EXCEPT returns rows from first result set that don't appear in second result set Common table expressions CTEs defined using WITH clause provide named temporary result sets that can be referenced within the main query Recursive CTEs allow hierarchical or recursive queries by referencing themselves'

specify what data they want to retrieve or manipulate rather than how to perform the operations The database management system DBMS is responsible for determining the most efficient way to execute SQL statements using query optimization techniques Chapter 2 Lexical Elements SQL statements are composed of various lexical elements including keywords identifiers literals operators and special characters Keywords are reserved words that have special meaning in SQL such as SELECT INSERT UPDATE DELETE CREATE DROP ALTER TABLE WHERE FROM JOIN ON AND OR NOT NULL TRUE FALSE Keywords are case-insensitive in most SQL implementations although some databases may treat them as case-sensitive Identifiers are names given to database objects such as tables columns indexes views procedures functions and triggers Identifiers must follow specific naming rules they typically must start with a letter and can contain letters digits and underscores The maximum length of identifiers varies by DBMS but is typically 128 or 255 characters Identifiers can be delimited using double quotes or backticks to allow special characters or reserved words to be used as names Literals represent constant values in SQL including numeric literals string literals date and time literals boolean literals and null literals Numeric literals can be integers such as 42 or floating-point numbers such as 3.14159 String literals are enclosed in single quotes such as 'Hello World' and can contain escape sequences for special characters Date and time literals follow ISO 8601 format such as DATE '2024-11-19' or TIMESTAMP '2024-11-19 05:30:00' Boolean literals are TRUE and FALSE while NULL represents the absence of a value Operators in SQL include arithmetic operators addition subtraction multiplication division modulo comparison operators equal not equal less than greater than less than or equal greater than or equal logical operators AND OR NOT string operators concatenation pattern matching set operators UNION INTERSECT EXCEPT and various other specialized operators Comments in SQL can be single-line comments starting with two hyphens -- and extending to the end of the line or multi-line comments enclosed in /* and */ delimiters Comments are ignored by the SQL parser and are used for documentation purposes Chapter 3 Data Types SQL supports various data types for storing different kinds of information Numeric data types include INTEGER INT SMALLINT BIGINT for whole numbers DECIMAL NUMERIC for fixed-precision numbers FLOAT REAL DOUBLE PRECISION for floating-point numbers Character string data types include CHAR CHARACTER for fixed-length strings VARCHAR CHARACTER VARYING for variable-length strings TEXT CLOB for large text objects Binary data types include BINARY VARBINARY BLOB for storing binary data Date and time data types include DATE for dates TIME for times TIMESTAMP for date and time combinations INTERVAL for time intervals Boolean data type BOOLEAN stores TRUE FALSE or NULL values Some databases also support specialized data types such as JSON XML UUID ARRAY geometric types network address types and user-defined types Chapter 4 Expressions and Predicates Expressions in SQL combine values operators and functions to produce results Value expressions can be column references literal values parameter markers function calls subqueries or complex expressions involving multiple operators Numeric expressions support standard arithmetic operations with operator precedence following mathematical conventions String expressions support concatenation using the || operator or CONCAT function substring extraction using SUBSTRING function case conversion using UPPER and LOWER functions trimming using TRIM LTRIM RTRIM functions and pattern matching using LIKE operator with wildcards percent sign for zero or more characters underscore for single character Date and time expressions support extraction of components using EXTRACT function arithmetic operations on dates and times using INTERVAL values formatting using various format functions and timezone conversions Predicates are expressions that evaluate to TRUE FALSE or UNKNOWN and are used primarily in WHERE clauses HAVING clauses and CHECK constraints Comparison predicates compare two values using operators equals not equals less than greater than less than or equal greater than or equal BETWEEN predicate tests whether a value falls within a range IN predicate tests whether a value matches any value in a list or subquery LIKE predicate performs pattern matching on strings using wildcards NULL predicate tests whether a value is NULL using IS NULL or IS NOT NULL EXISTS predicate tests whether a subquery returns any rows Quantified predicates use ALL ANY SOME with comparison operators and subqueries Logical operators AND OR NOT combine predicates with three-valued logic handling NULL values Chapter 5 Query Expressions The SELECT statement is the primary means of retrieving data from databases A basic SELECT statement consists of SELECT clause specifying columns to retrieve FROM clause specifying tables to query from WHERE clause specifying conditions for filtering rows GROUP BY clause for grouping rows HAVING clause for filtering groups ORDER BY clause for sorting results LIMIT clause for limiting number of rows returned The SELECT clause can include column names expressions aggregate functions window functions and the asterisk wildcard for all columns Column aliases can be specified using AS keyword or simply by following the expression with the alias name The FROM clause specifies one or more tables views or subqueries to retrieve data from Multiple tables can be joined using various join types INNER JOIN returns only matching rows from both tables LEFT OUTER JOIN returns all rows from left table and matching rows from right table RIGHT OUTER JOIN returns all rows from right table and matching rows from left table FULL OUTER JOIN returns all rows from both tables CROSS JOIN returns Cartesian product of both tables Join conditions are specified using ON clause or USING clause for natural joins The WHERE clause filters rows based on predicates and can include complex conditions combining multiple predicates with logical operators Subqueries can be used in WHERE clause for correlated or non-correlated filtering The GROUP BY clause groups rows that have the same values in specified columns Aggregate functions COUNT SUM AVG MIN MAX are applied to each group The HAVING clause filters groups based on aggregate conditions The ORDER BY clause sorts the result set by one or more columns in ascending ASC or descending DESC order NULL values are sorted either first or last depending on database configuration Window functions perform calculations across sets of rows related to the current row without collapsing the result set like aggregate functions Window functions include ranking functions ROW_NUMBER RANK DENSE_RANK NTILE aggregate functions used as window functions SUM AVG COUNT MIN MAX and value functions LAG LEAD FIRST_VALUE LAST_VALUE Window specifications define the window frame using PARTITION BY for partitioning ORDER BY for ordering and frame clauses ROWS or RANGE for defining frame boundaries Set operations combine results from multiple SELECT statements UNION combines results removing duplicates UNION ALL combines results keeping duplicates INTERSECT returns only rows that appear in both result sets EXCEPT returns rows from first result set that don't appear in second result set Common table expressions CTEs defined using WITH clause provide named temporary result sets that can be referenced within the main query Recursive CTEs allow hierarchical or recursive queries by referencing themselves

that are correctly detected F1-score the harmonic mean of precision and recall false positive rate the proportion of benign queries incorrectly classified as malicious false negative rate the proportion of malicious queries incorrectly classified as benign area under ROC curve AUC a measure of overall classification performance training time the time required to train the model inference latency the time required to classify a single query throughput the number of queries that can be classified per second memory usage the amount of RAM required during operation and model size the storage space required for the trained model For machine learning and deep learning systems the evaluation includes 10-fold cross-validation repeated 5 times to ensure statistical reliability Results are reported as mean values with standard deviations The evaluation also includes ablation studies to understand the contribution of different components feature engineering techniques and hyperparameters Rule-Based Systems Performance Rule-based systems use predefined patterns and signatures to detect SQL injection attacks These systems include web application firewalls intrusion detection systems and specialized SQL injection detection tools The evaluation includes 8 rule-based systems representing both open-source and commercial products ModSecurity with Core Rule Set CRS version 4.0 achieves accuracy of 87.3% with standard deviation of 1.2% across multiple runs The system demonstrates precision of 82.1% meaning that 17.9% of queries flagged as malicious are actually benign resulting in false positives that may impact legitimate users The recall is 78.5% indicating that 21.5% of actual attacks are not detected leaving significant security gaps The F1-score of 80.3% reflects the balance between precision and recall The false positive rate is 8.9% which translates to approximately 36,000 false alarms per day in a system processing 10 million queries daily The false negative rate of 21.5% means that more than one in five attacks will bypass detection The inference latency is 3.2 milliseconds per query with throughput of 312 queries per second on a single CPU core Memory usage is minimal at 45 MB and the rule set size is 2.8 MB PHPIDS version 0.7 achieves lower accuracy of 84.7% with precision of 79.8% and recall of 75.2% The F1-score is 77.4% with false positive rate of 10.3% and false negative rate of 24.8% The inference latency is higher at 5.1 milliseconds per query with throughput of 196 queries per second Memory usage is 67 MB and rule set size is 1.2 MB The higher latency is attributed to more complex regular expression matching and additional preprocessing steps Snort with SQL injection detection rules achieves accuracy of 81.2% with precision of 76.4% and recall of 71.8% The F1-score is 74.0% with false positive rate of 12.1% and false negative rate of 28.2% The inference latency is 2.8 milliseconds per query with throughput of 357 queries per second Memory usage is 38 MB and rule set size is 890 KB The relatively better performance in terms of latency is due to optimized pattern matching algorithms Suricata with emerging threats SQL injection rules achieves accuracy of 83.5% with precision of 78.9% and recall of 73.6% The F1-score is 76.2% with false positive rate of 11.4% and false negative rate of 26.4% The inference latency is 3.5 milliseconds per query with throughput of 286 queries per second Memory usage is 52 MB and rule set size is 1.5 MB Custom rule-based system developed specifically for this evaluation using manually crafted rules achieves accuracy of 89.1% with precision of 85.3% and recall of 81.7% The F1-score is 83.5% with false positive rate of 7.2% and false negative rate of 18.3% The inference latency is 4.2 milliseconds per query with throughput of 238 queries per second Memory usage is 78 MB and rule set size is 3.4 MB The improved accuracy comes from more comprehensive rules but at the cost of higher computational overhead Analysis of rule-based systems reveals several patterns First accuracy is limited by the coverage of rules systems can only detect attacks that match predefined patterns Second false positive rates tend to be high because rules often use broad patterns that match legitimate queries Third false negative rates are significant because attackers can evade rules using encoding obfuscation and other techniques Fourth computational efficiency is generally good with low latency and memory usage Fifth these systems require continuous rule updates to detect new attack variants Sixth the effectiveness varies significantly across different attack types with good detection of simple attacks but poor detection of sophisticated evasion techniques Machine Learning Systems Performance Machine learning systems use statistical models trained on labeled data to classify SQL queries as benign or malicious The evaluation includes 12 machine learning systems using various algorithms and feature engineering approaches Decision tree classifier using CART algorithm with maximum depth of 15 and minimum samples per leaf of 10 achieves accuracy of 91.4% with precision of 88.7% and recall of 85.3% The F1-score is 87.0% with false positive rate of 5.8% and false negative rate of 14.7% The training time is 23 seconds on the full training set The inference latency is 0.8 milliseconds per query with throughput of 1,250 queries per second Memory usage during inference is 156 MB and model size is 42 MB The decision tree uses 8,347 nodes with average depth of 12.3 Feature importance analysis reveals that the most important features are the presence of SQL keywords union select where the number of SQL operators the ratio of special characters to total characters and the query length Random forest classifier with 200 trees maximum depth of 20 and minimum samples per leaf of 5 achieves accuracy of
