click Network select your active network connection click Advanced navigate to the Proxies tab check Web Proxy HTTP and Secure Web Proxy HTTPS enter 127.0.0.1 as the Web Proxy Server and 8080 as the port and click OK After configuring your browser proxy you need to install Burp Suite's CA certificate to intercept HTTPS traffic Without the CA certificate your browser will display security warnings for HTTPS sites because it doesn't trust Burp Suite's certificate To install the certificate configure your browser to use Burp Suite as a proxy then navigate to http://burpsuite in your browser This will display the Burp Suite start page where you can click CA Certificate to download the certificate file For Firefox open Settings navigate to Privacy & Security scroll down to Certificates click View Certificates click the Authorities tab click Import select the downloaded certificate file check Trust this CA to identify websites and click OK For Chrome and other browsers that use the system certificate store you need to import the certificate into your operating system's certificate store For Windows double-click the certificate file click Install Certificate select Current User or Local Machine click Next select Place all certificates in the following store click Browse select Trusted Root Certification Authorities click OK and complete the wizard For macOS double-click the certificate file which will open Keychain Access select System or login keychain click Add find the certificate in the list double-click it expand Trust select Always Trust for When using this certificate and close the window Proxy Tool The Proxy tool is the core component of Burp Suite that allows you to intercept view and modify HTTP and HTTPS requests and responses The Proxy tab contains several sub-tabs including Intercept which allows you to intercept and modify individual requests and responses HTTP history which displays all HTTP traffic that has passed through the proxy WebSockets history which displays WebSocket communications and Options which contains various proxy configuration settings The Intercept sub-tab allows you to control whether Burp Suite intercepts requests and responses When interception is enabled Burp Suite will pause each request or response and display it in the Intercept tab allowing you to view and modify it before forwarding it to its destination You can toggle interception on and off using the Intercept is on/off button When a request or response is intercepted you can view its details including the HTTP method URL headers and body You can modify any part of the intercepted message by editing it directly in the text editor After making your modifications you can click Forward to send the modified message to its destination Drop to discard the message or Action to perform various actions such as sending the message to other Burp Suite tools The HTTP history sub-tab displays a complete log of all HTTP traffic that has passed through the proxy Each entry shows the request number time method URL status code length MIME type and other details You can click on any entry to view the full request and response including headers and body The history can be filtered using various criteria such as showing only in-scope items items with specific status codes or items matching specific search terms You can also annotate history items with comments and highlights to help organize your testing The Options sub-tab contains numerous configuration settings for the proxy including proxy listeners which define the interfaces and ports that Burp Suite listens on for incoming connections intercept client requests and intercept server responses which allow you to configure rules for automatically intercepting or forwarding messages based on various criteria response modification which allows you to automatically modify responses such as unhiding hidden form fields or removing JavaScript that interferes with testing match and replace which allows you to define rules for automatically replacing parts of requests or responses and SSL pass through which allows you to configure specific hosts where SSL connections should be passed through without interception Target Tool The Target tool helps you define and organize the scope of your testing and provides detailed information about the target application The Target tab contains two sub-tabs Site map which displays a hierarchical view of all content discovered on the target application and Scope which allows you to define which hosts and URLs are in scope for your testing The Site map displays all URLs that Burp Suite has observed organized in a tree structure by protocol host and path For each item in the site map you can view details including the HTTP request and response the number of requests made to that URL and any issues that have been identified You can expand and collapse branches of the tree to navigate through the application structure The site map can be filtered to show only in-scope items items with specific response codes or items matching specific search terms You can also manually add items to the site map by right-clicking and selecting Add item The Scope sub-tab allows you to define which targets are in scope for your testing Defining scope is important because it allows you to focus on the specific targets you are authorized to test and exclude out-of-scope targets such as third-party sites You can add items to scope by entering URL prefixes or using advanced scope control which allows you to define scope using protocol host port and file patterns You can also add items to scope directly from other Burp Suite tools by right-clicking on requests and selecting Add to scope Burp Suite will prompt you whether to stop logging out-of-scope items which can help reduce clutter in your proxy history and site map Scanner Tool The Scanner tool automatically crawls and scans web applications to identify security vulnerabilities Burp Suite Professional includes an advanced web vulnerability scanner that can detect a wide range of issues including SQL injection cross-site scripting command injection path traversal file inclusion and many others The Scanner tab contains several sub-tabs including Scan queue which displays active and completed scans Issue activity which shows issues as they are discovered Issue definitions which provides detailed information about each type of vulnerability and Options which contains scanner configuration settings To start a scan you can right-click on any item in the site map proxy history or other tool and select Scan or Do active scan or Do passive scan Active scanning sends requests to the application to probe for vulnerabilities and may modify application state while passive scanning only analyzes existing traffic without sending additional requests The Scan queue sub-tab displays all active and queued scans showing the target URL scan type status progress and number of requests made You can pause resume or cancel scans and configure various scan settings such as the scan speed and resource limits The Issue activity sub-tab displays all vulnerabilities discovered by the scanner organized by severity high medium low and informational For each issue you can view detailed information including the issue type description affected URL vulnerability evidence remediation advice and references to additional information You can also mark issues as false positives or add comments to track your testing progress The Scanner Options sub-tab contains extensive configuration settings for controlling scanner behavior including attack insertion points which define where the scanner will inject payloads active scanning optimization which controls the speed and thoroughness of scanning active scanning areas which allows you to enable or disable specific vulnerability checks passive scanning which controls what passive checks are performed and static code analysis which integrates with Burp Suite's JavaScript analysis capabilities Intruder Tool The Intruder tool allows you to perform automated customized attacks against web applications such as fuzzing testing for vulnerabilities and extracting data The Intruder tool is highly flexible and can be used for a wide variety of testing scenarios including brute force attacks testing for SQL injection and XSS extracting useful data from responses and fuzzing for application errors The Intruder tab contains several sub-tabs including Target which specifies the target host and port Positions which defines where payloads will be inserted in the request Payloads which configures the payloads to be used in the attack Options which contains various attack configuration settings and Results which displays the results of the attack To use Intruder you first need to send a request to Intruder by right-clicking on a request in another tool and selecting Send to Intruder The request will appear in the Intruder Target tab showing the target host and port In the Positions tab you define where in the request you want to insert payloads by placing payload markers around the relevant parts of the request Burp Suite will automatically mark common injection points such as parameter values but you can manually add remove or modify payload positions The Positions tab also allows you to select the attack type which determines how multiple payload positions are handled Sniper uses a single payload set and places each payload into each position in turn Battering ram uses a single payload set and places the same payload into all positions simultaneously Pitchfork uses multiple payload sets and places payloads into positions in parallel using one payload from each set per request and Cluster bomb uses multiple payload sets and tries all combinations of payloads across all positions In the Payloads tab you configure the payloads to be used in the attack Burp Suite supports numerous payload types including simple list which uses a predefined list of strings runtime file which loads payloads from a file at runtime custom iterator which generates payloads by combining items from multiple lists character substitution which generates payloads by substituting characters in a base string case modification which generates case variations of a base string recursive grep which extracts payloads from previous responses illegal Unicode which generates various Unicode encodings character blocks which generates strings of a specific character numbers which generates sequential or random numbers dates which generates date values brute forcer which generates all possible strings of a given character set and length null payloads which generates empty payloads username generator which generates common username formats and ECB block shuffler which manipulates encrypted data For each payload type you can configure various settings such as the payload list character set number range or extraction pattern The Options tab contains numerous settings for controlling attack behavior including request headers which allows you to modify headers for each request request engine which controls the number of concurrent requests and timing between requests grep match which extracts and displays specific strings from responses grep extract which extracts data from responses using start and end markers grep payloads which highlights responses containing the payload redirections which controls how redirections are handled and results which controls what information is displayed in the results The Results tab displays the results of the attack showing each request number payload status code error length time and other details You can sort and filter results to identify interesting responses such as those with different status codes lengths or content You can click on any result to view the full request and response and you can mark results with comments and highlights

uses database sleep functions to create observable delays The year 2007 marked the beginning of large-scale automated SQL injection attacks targeting thousands of websites simultaneously Attackers used botnets to scan the internet for vulnerable sites and automatically inject malicious code into database tables which would then be served to website visitors infecting them with malware These language TCL statements SQL is designed to be declarative meaning that users specify what data they want to retrieve or manipulate rather than how to perform the operations The database management lexical elements including keywords identifiers literals operators and special characters Keywords are reserved words that have special meaning in SQL such as SELECT INSERT UPDATE DELETE CREATE DROP ALTER TABLE WHERE FROM JOIN ON AND OR NOT NULL TRUE FALSE Keywords are case-insensitive in most SQL implementations although some databases may treat them as case-sensitive Identifiers are names given and time literals follow ISO 8601 format such as DATE '2024-11-19' or TIMESTAMP '2024-11-19 05:30:00' Boolean literals are TRUE and FALSE while NULL represents the absence of a value Operators in SQL include arithmetic operators addition subtraction multiplication division modulo comparison operators equal not equal less than greater than less than or equal greater than or equal logical operators AND OR NOT string operators concatenation pattern matching set operators UNION INTERSECT EXCEPT and various other specialized operators Comments in SQL can be single-line comments starting with two hyphens -- and extending to the end of the line or multi-line comments enclosed in /* and */ delimiters Comments are ignored by the SQL parser and are used for documentation purposes Chapter 3 Data Types SQL supports various data types for storing different kinds of information Numeric data types include INTEGER INT SMALLINT BIGINT for whole numbers DECIMAL NUMERIC for fixed-precision numbers FLOAT REAL DOUBLE PRECISION for floating-point numbers Character string data types include CHAR CHARACTER for fixed-length strings VARCHAR CHARACTER VARYING for variable-length strings TEXT CLOB for large text objects Binary data types include BINARY VARBINARY BLOB for storing binary data Date and time data types include DATE for dates TIME for times TIMESTAMP for date and time combinations INTERVAL for time intervals Boolean data type BOOLEAN stores TRUE FALSE or NULL values Some databases also support specialized data types such as JSON XML UUID ARRAY geometric types network address types and user-defined types Chapter 4 Expressions and Predicates Expressions in SQL combine values operators and functions to produce results Value expressions can be column references literal values trimming using TRIM LTRIM RTRIM functions and pattern matching using LIKE operator with wildcards percent sign for zero or more characters underscore for single character Date and time expressions support extraction of components using EXTRACT function arithmetic operations on dates and times using INTERVAL values formatting using various format functions and timezone conversions Predicates are expressions that evaluate to TRUE FALSE or UNKNOWN and are used primarily in WHERE clauses HAVING clauses and CHECK constraints Comparison predicates compare two values using operators equals not equals less than greater than less than or equal greater than or equal BETWEEN predicate tests whether a value falls within a range IN predicate tests whether a value matches any value in a list or subquery LIKE predicate performs pattern matching on strings using wildcards NULL predicate tests whether a value is NULL using IS NULL or IS NOT NULL EXISTS predicate tests whether a subquery returns any rows Quantified predicates use ALL ANY SOME with comparison operators and subqueries Logical operators AND OR NOT combine predicates with three-valued logic handling NULL values Chapter 5 Query Expressions The SELECT statement is the primary means of retrieving data from databases A basic SELECT statement consists of SELECT clause specifying columns to retrieve FROM clause specifying tables to query from WHERE clause specifying conditions for filtering rows GROUP BY clause for grouping rows HAVING clause for filtering groups ORDER BY clause for sorting results LIMIT clause for limiting number of rows returned The SELECT clause can include column names expressions aggregate functions window functions and the asterisk wildcard for all columns Column aliases can be specified using AS keyword or simply by following the expression with the alias name The FROM clause specifies one or more tables views or subqueries to retrieve data from Multiple tables can be joined using various join types INNER JOIN returns only matching rows from both tables LEFT OUTER JOIN returns all rows from left table and matching rows from right table RIGHT OUTER JOIN returns all rows from right table and matching rows from left table FULL OUTER JOIN returns all rows from both tables CROSS JOIN returns Cartesian product of both tables Join conditions are specified using ON clause or USING clause for natural joins The WHERE clause filters rows based on predicates and can include complex conditions combining multiple predicates with logical operators Subqueries can be used in WHERE clause for correlated or non-correlated filtering The GROUP BY clause groups rows that have the same values in specified columns Aggregate functions COUNT SUM AVG MIN MAX are applied to each group The HAVING clause filters groups based on aggregate conditions The ORDER BY clause sorts the result set by one or more columns in ascending ASC or descending DESC order NULL values are sorted either first or last depending on database configuration Window functions perform calculations across sets of rows related to the current row without collapsing the result set like aggregate functions Window functions include ranking functions ROW_NUMBER RANK DENSE_RANK NTILE aggregate functions used as window functions SUM AVG COUNT MIN MAX and value functions LAG LEAD FIRST_VALUE LAST_VALUE Window specifications define the window frame using PARTITION BY for partitioning ORDER BY for ordering and frame clauses ROWS or RANGE for defining frame boundaries Set operations combine results from multiple SELECT statements UNION combines results removing duplicates UNION ALL combines results keeping duplicates INTERSECT returns only rows that appear in both result sets EXCEPT returns rows from first result set that don't appear in second result set Common table expressions CTEs defined using WITH clause provide named temporary result sets that can be referenced within the main query Recursive CTEs allow hierarchical or recursive queries by referencing themselves'

unique challenges for SQL injection prevention and detection In 2022 researchers discovered SQL injection vulnerabilities in artificial intelligence and machine learning systems particularly in
